## Attention Head Structure and Cache-Efficient Variants {#sec-ch3}

*Why Fewer Key/Value Heads Means a Smaller Cache -- Not a Smaller Model*

### Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- Distinguish query-head count ($H_q$) from key/value-head count
  ($H_{kv}$), and write $Q$/$K$/$V$'s shapes before and after splitting
  into heads.
- Explain how multiple query heads can share a key/value head, and
  distinguish MHA, MQA, and GQA structurally on that one axis.
- Calculate a decoder's logical KV-cache size under stated assumptions,
  and state which projection parameters change when $H_{kv}$ changes
  (and which don't).
- Explain why reducing $H_{kv}$ lowers cache memory and memory traffic
  without reducing every part of attention computation by the same
  factor.
- Identify tradeoffs among MHA, MQA, and GQA without claiming any one
  is universally best, and distinguish an architecture-level cache
  calculation from measured serving-memory usage.

### Why this matters

Chapters 1-2 gave every block one query head per key/value head,
without saying that was a choice. It is. The number of key/value heads
a model uses is an independent design knob from the number of query
heads, and it is the single knob most responsible for how much memory
autoregressive decoding needs per active sequence. Get this chapter's
distinction wrong and two very different mistakes follow: overstating
what changes (claiming a smaller cache means a proportionally smaller
or faster model) or understating it (missing that cache memory, not
FLOPs, is usually the actual serving bottleneck this chapter is about).

### Mental model or analogy

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy"}
Queries are readers asking different questions; keys are index entries
used to decide where to look; values are the information retrieved at
that index entry. Standard attention (MHA) gives every reader their
own private index and information store. MQA makes all readers share
one shared index and store. GQA gives each *group* of readers a shared
index and store -- a middle ground between the two.

**Where this breaks down:** keys and values are learned vector
projections, not literal documents. Sharing a key/value head changes
how much distinct *representational capacity* the model has to work
with, not merely how many copies of a document are stored -- two
readers sharing an index can no longer each shape that index around
only their own question.
:::

### Technical core

This chapter uses $H_q$ (query heads), $H_{kv}$ (key/value heads),
$d_{\text{head}}$ (head dimension, with $d_{\text{model}} = H_q \,
d_{\text{head}}$), $S$ (tokens retained in the cache), $T_q$ (query
positions processed in the *current* step -- $T_q = S$ during prefill,
$T_q = 1$ for an ordinary decode step), $L$ (layers), and
$\text{bytes\_per\_elem}$ (storage width per cached number, e.g. 2 for
bf16). Logical shapes, head axis explicit (physical memory layouts
vary by implementation):

$$
Q: (B, T_q, H_q, d_{\text{head}}), \qquad
K: (B, S, H_{kv}, d_{\text{head}}), \qquad
V: (B, S, H_{kv}, d_{\text{head}})
$$ {#eq-qkv-head-shapes}

**MHA, MQA, GQA: one axis, three points.** Standard multi-head
attention (MHA, [@src-19]) sets $H_{kv} = H_q$: every query head has
its own key/value head. Multi-query attention (MQA, [@src-20]) sets
$H_{kv} = 1$: every query head shares the same single key/value head.
Grouped-query attention (GQA, [@src-21]) sets $1 < H_{kv} < H_q$: query
heads are split into $H_q / H_{kv}$ equal groups (this simple
equal-group presentation requires $H_{kv}$ to divide $H_q$), each group
sharing one key/value head. @fig-head-sharing shows all three at
$H_q = 8$.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"GQA reduces the number of query heads."** It does not. $H_q$ is
untouched by any of these three variants -- @fig-head-sharing draws the
same 8 query heads in every panel. Only $H_{kv}$ changes.
:::

**What stays fixed, what changes.** Across MHA/MQA/GQA at the same
$H_q$ and $d_{\text{head}}$: the query projection's shape, the
per-head attention *output* shape, the concatenated output width, and
the output projection width are all unchanged -- every one of them
depends on $H_q$, not $H_{kv}$. What changes is the $K$/$V$
projections' output width and, per position, how many $K$/$V$ vectors
get stored. @fig-tensor-shape-gqa marks the one shape that differs.

![Only $K$/$V$'s head axis ($H_{kv}$) shrinks between MHA and GQA;
$Q$'s shape is untouched.](figures/rendered/fig-tensor-shape-gqa.svg){#fig-tensor-shape-gqa}

**Projection parameters.** Ignoring biases, per layer:

$$
P_Q = d_{\text{model}} \, H_q \, d_{\text{head}}, \quad
P_K = d_{\text{model}} \, H_{kv} \, d_{\text{head}}, \quad
P_V = d_{\text{model}} \, H_{kv} \, d_{\text{head}}, \quad
P_O = H_q \, d_{\text{head}} \, d_{\text{model}}
$$ {#eq-attn-proj-params}

Only $P_K$ and $P_V$ depend on $H_{kv}$; $P_Q$ and $P_O$ depend only on
$H_q$. Shrinking $H_{kv}$ shrinks two of these four terms, not all
four -- the worked example below turns this into a concrete ratio.

**KV-cache size.** The quantity these mechanisms actually optimize is
not parameter count but cache memory:

$$
M_{KV} = 2 \, B \, S \, L \, H_{kv} \, d_{\text{head}} \,
\text{bytes\_per\_elem}
$$ {#eq-kv-cache}

where the factor 2 counts keys *and* values. This is a **logical,
theoretical minimum** -- under this workbook's distinction between logical
and measured memory, it explicitly excludes allocator overhead,
block/page metadata, fragmentation, temporary attention workspaces,
framework buffers, duplicated or padded storage, sharding-specific
per-device layouts, prefix-sharing effects, and any cache quantization
not already reflected in $\text{bytes\_per\_elem}$.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"The KV-cache formula gives exact observed GPU memory usage."** It
does not. @eq-kv-cache is a logical minimum computed from a config;
what `nvidia-smi` or a profiler reports also includes every exclusion
listed above, and will always be larger.
:::

**Decode-time computation.** At each decode step, $T_q$ new query
positions are computed (ordinarily $T_q = 1$; chunked prefill and
speculative-decoding verification -- both later topics, named here only
as forward references -- can make $T_q > 1$). Every one of the $H_q$
query heads still produces its own attention scores; a shared
key/value head is simply reused (logically broadcast) across every
query head in its group. Reducing $H_{kv}$ principally reduces what
gets *stored* and *moved* -- it does not reduce the number of
query-side dot products, so it is not accurate to say GQA makes
attention some fixed multiple faster; the win this chapter is about is
memory and memory-bandwidth, not FLOPs.

### Worked example

**KV-cache memory.** Base config: $L = 32$, $H_q = 32$,
$d_{\text{head}} = 128$ (so $d_{\text{model}} = 4096$), $S = 8192$,
$B = 1$, bf16 ($\text{bytes\_per\_elem} = 2$) -- verified
programmatically (see the Build and Version Note):

| Variant | $H_{kv}$ | @eq-kv-cache result | vs. MHA |
|---|---|---|---|
| MHA | 32 | 4,294,967,296 B = 4 GiB | 1x |
| GQA | 8 | 1,073,741,824 B = 1 GiB | 0.25x (4x smaller) |
| MQA | 1 | 134,217,728 B = 128 MiB | 0.03125x (32x smaller) |

: KV-cache size for one sequence at $S=8192$; the reduction factor equals $H_{kv,\text{variant}} / H_{kv,\text{MHA}}$ exactly {#tbl-kv-cache-worked}

![The same three numbers as @tbl-kv-cache-worked -- bar height is
log2-scaled so the smallest bar stays visible; the printed values are
the actual linear byte
counts.](figures/rendered/fig-kv-cache-scaling.svg){#fig-kv-cache-scaling}

Cache size scales *linearly* in each of $B$, $S$, $L$, $H_{kv}$, and
$\text{bytes\_per\_elem}$ -- e.g. at $B = 16$ active sequences instead
of 1, every number in @tbl-kv-cache-worked simply multiplies by 16 (4
GiB $\to$ 64 GiB for MHA, 1 GiB $\to$ 16 GiB for GQA, 128 MiB $\to$ 2
GiB for MQA); nothing about the formula's *shape* changes.

**Projection parameters, same config.** Per layer, from @eq-attn-proj-params:

| Variant | $P_Q$ | $P_K$+$P_V$ | $P_O$ | Total ($Q$+$K$+$V$+$O$) | $K$+$V$ vs. MHA | Total vs. MHA |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MHA | 16,777,216 | 33,554,432 | 16,777,216 | 67,108,864 | 1x | 1x |
| GQA | 16,777,216 | 8,388,608 | 16,777,216 | 41,943,040 | 0.25x | 0.625x |
| MQA | 16,777,216 | 1,048,576 | 16,777,216 | 34,603,008 | 0.03125x | 0.516x |

: Per-layer attention parameters for the same base config -- $K$+$V$ shrinks by exactly the cache-reduction ratio, but the complete attention block (which also includes $Q$ and $O$, both fixed) shrinks by much less {#tbl-proj-params-worked}

GQA's $K$+$V$ parameters drop by exactly 4x, matching its cache
reduction -- but the *complete* attention block (adding the unchanged
$P_Q$ and $P_O$) drops by only 1.6x (to 0.625 of MHA's total), and MQA's
32x $K$+$V$ reduction becomes less than a 2x reduction (0.516x) once
$Q$ and $O$ are included. This is @eq-attn-proj-params's point made
concrete: $K$/$V$ savings do not translate one-for-one into
whole-model or whole-attention-block savings.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"If GQA cuts KV-cache memory by 4x, the whole model becomes 4x
smaller."** @tbl-proj-params-worked shows why not: the complete
attention block's parameters (which include the unchanged $Q$ and $O$
projections) shrink by only 1.6x here, and the feed-forward sublayers
(chapters 1-2) are untouched by $H_{kv}$ entirely.
:::

### Compare and contrast

| | MHA | GQA | MQA |
|---|---|---|---|
| $H_{kv}$ | $H_{kv} = H_q$ | $1 < H_{kv} < H_q$ | $H_{kv} = 1$ |
| $K$/$V$ sharing | none | groups of $H_q/H_{kv}$ query heads | all query heads |
| Logical KV-cache size | largest (1x) | intermediate (config-dependent) | smallest (1x/$H_q$) |
| $K$/$V$ projection params | largest | intermediate | smallest |
| Representation flexibility | most (every head has its own $K$/$V$) | reduced, tunable via group size | least |
| Implementation considerations | simplest; no grouping logic | requires choosing a group size that divides $H_q$ | simplest sharing case; largest capacity reduction |
| Common motivation | small models, or when cache memory isn't the bottleneck | a tunable memory/flexibility tradeoff point | maximum cache/bandwidth savings when acceptable |

: MHA vs. GQA vs. MQA, compared without ranking one as strictly best -- each row is a tradeoff, not a verdict {#tbl-variant-comparison}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"MQA is universally superior because it uses the least cache."**
Least cache is not the only deployment factor. MQA gives every query
head the least representational flexibility of the three (all of them
share one key/value head, with no group boundary at all), which is
exactly the tradeoff [@src-21] introduces GQA to soften -- reducing $H_{kv}$
buys memory at a flexibility cost, and where that cost is acceptable is
model- and workload-dependent, not a fixed rule.
:::

### Applied exercise

A serving workload needs long contexts and high concurrency. Candidate
model A uses MHA; candidate B uses GQA, both otherwise the same size
and $S$. Using @eq-kv-cache, compare their per-sequence cache cost at
your own chosen (long) $S$ and (large) $B$, then explicitly name at
least one deployment factor besides cache memory (e.g. representation
flexibility, implementation maturity, quality at the model's specific
task) that could still favor the MHA candidate despite its larger
cache. A serving decision is not a cache-size comparison alone.

### Interview lens

*"Walk me through why GQA reduces KV-cache cost, and tell me what it
does not automatically make cheaper."* A strong answer names $H_{kv}$
(not $H_q$) as the changing quantity, states @eq-kv-cache's linear
dependence on $H_{kv}$, and explicitly names what does *not* shrink
proportionally: the query and output projections ($P_Q$, $P_O$), the
number of query-side attention computations, and (per
@tbl-proj-params-worked) the complete attention block's total
parameter count. An answer that only says "it uses less memory"
without naming what stays fixed is incomplete for a systems-flavored
interview.

### Chapter recap

- $H_q$ and $H_{kv}$ are independent: MHA sets $H_{kv}=H_q$, MQA sets
  $H_{kv}=1$, GQA sets $1<H_{kv}<H_q$ -- the same head-sharing axis at
  three points, never fewer query heads.
- Only the $K$/$V$ projections' shape and the KV-cache size depend on
  $H_{kv}$; $Q$'s shape, the output projection, and the number of
  query-side attention computations depend on $H_q$ alone.
- The KV-cache formula ($2 \times B \times S \times L \times H_{kv}
  \times d_{\text{head}} \times \text{bytes\_per\_elem}$) is a logical
  minimum, not a measured GPU-memory number.
- $K$/$V$ parameter and cache savings do not translate one-for-one into
  whole-model or whole-attention-block savings, and reducing $H_{kv}$
  does not proportionally cut attention FLOPs.
- None of MHA, GQA, or MQA is universally best -- each trades cache
  memory against representational flexibility differently.

### Sources and further reading

Primary sources for this chapter: [@src-19] for the MHA baseline,
[@src-20] for MQA, [@src-21] for GQA (including its uptraining recipe
for converting an existing MHA checkpoint, reported at roughly 5% of
original pretraining compute -- their own reported figure, not a
universal constant). Secondary/supporting: [@src-14] for cross-model
framing, [@src-10] for the KV-cache memory formula's systems framing.
A further latent-compression technique that shrinks the cache by a
different mechanism than head-sharing exists and is left for the next
chapter, not covered here.
